extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for structuring individual scenes and their follow-ups (sequels) in fiction to maintain pacing, build tension, develop characters, and advance plot. Teaches the Goal–Conflict–Disaster scene pattern and the Reaction–Dilemma–Decision sequel pattern and how to alternate them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scene (Goal–Conflict–Disaster)
rubrics_metrics.description: A scene has the following pattern: Goal – what the character wants (must be clearly definable); Conflict – an obstacle or series of obstacles that keep the character from the goal; Disaster – makes the character fail to get the goal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scenes should be driven by a clear, definable goal and include escalating obstacles that culminate in a disaster (failure). Use this to create forward motion and stakes; a proper disaster provokes emotional reaction and sets up the following sequel.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sequel (Reaction–Dilemma–Decision)
rubrics_metrics.description: A sequel has the following pattern: Reaction – emotional follow through of the disaster; Dilemma – a situation with no good options; Decision – character makes a choice (which sets up the new goal).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sequels allow characters (and readers) to process the scene’s disaster, evaluate options, and make a decision that establishes the next scene’s goal. Use sequels for character development and to justify shifts in direction or new objectives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alternate between Scene and Sequel
rubrics_metrics.description: Alternate between the two variant types of scenes known as SCENE and SEQUEL: the SCENE is driven by goal, conflict, and disaster; it is then followed by a SEQUEL, which contains reaction, dilemma, and decision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Alternation produces a steady, consistent pacing and a repeating cycle where each decision leads to a new goal and thus the next scene. This pattern helps maintain reading speed and prevents portions of the novel from lagging or dragging.

rubrics_metrics.name: Goal must be clearly definable
rubrics_metrics.description: Goal – what the character wants. Must be clearly definable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A clearly defined goal is essential to motivate the character’s actions and to make the stakes and conflict understandable to the reader. Vague or fuzzy goals weaken scenes and reduce tension.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conflict should present real obstacles
rubrics_metrics.description: Conflict – an obstacle or series of obstacles that keep the character from the goal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conflict should be meaningful and escalate within the scene. Use obstacles that challenge the character and reveal character traits; avoid superficial or convenience-based obstacles that fail to pressure the protagonist.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disaster must result in failure or setback
rubrics_metrics.description: Disaster – makes the character fail to get the goal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The disaster (or setback) at the end of a scene should decisively prevent the character from achieving the goal, forcing emotional consequences and narrative change that the sequel can address. Weak or reversible disasters reduce dramatic impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reaction should show emotional follow-through
rubrics_metrics.description: Reaction – emotional follow through of the disaster.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sequels should include believable emotional responses that let readers process the consequences. Showing inner life here deepens character, prevents pacing monotony, and connects readers to the stakes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dilemma should present no good options
rubrics_metrics.description: Dilemma – a situation with no good options.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The dilemma forces the character to choose under pressure; presenting only bad or costly choices heightens tension and reveals priorities. Avoid easy or obvious choices that undercut the sequel’s purpose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decision must set a new goal and forward the plot
rubrics_metrics.description: Decision – character makes a choice (which sets up the new goal).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decisions made in sequels should logically produce the next scene’s goal, creating a causal chain. Ensure choices are motivated by the character’s reactions and dilemmas so the cycle of scene→sequel→scene feels organic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use Scene-and-Sequel to maintain pacing and emotional engagement
rubrics_metrics.description: Scene and Sequel is a technique to help create solid pacing while also guiding you to account for factors that build tension, develop characters, describe setting, and advance plot lines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Alternate scenes and sequels to keep a steady reading speed and to avoid sections that lag or fail to create a deep emotional connection. The pattern helps balance action with reaction, ensuring the novel advances plot while deepening character and atmosphere.
